narrative:
The model estimates that you have a 68 percent chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. That is more than two out of three, a high level of risk, and it is why your law school application was denied.

Three factors, in order of importance, drove this decision. The strongest signal was your class standing in your third year. You are in the first decile of your class, meaning you finished among the lowest ten percent that year. By contrast, students who were accepted typically sit around the sixth decile. This pattern indicates that your performance near the end of your undergraduate studies was not on the path expected for bar readiness.

The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 18, it is well below the average of about 37 among accepted students. The LSAT measures reasoning skills that are directly related to succeeding on the bar exam, so a low score is a serious concern.

Your undergraduate GPA was actually a point in your favor. It nudged the prediction toward passing the bar, not failing it. However, your GPA of 3.20 is essentially the same as the typical accepted student's 3.23, so it could not compensate for the weaknesses in your class rank and LSAT.

What can you do now? Focus on strengthening the areas that mattered most. Consider retaking the LSAT after dedicated preparation, and enroll in further coursework that allows you to demonstrate a higher class rank. If you can show stronger academic performance and a competitive LSAT score, your next application will present a very different picture.
